channel.title: BotsDoThat: new AI agent use cases
channel.description: BotsDoThat Today: every weekday, the 3 changes in AI assistants that matter for everyday users, what each means for you, and one job to try with a copy-paste prompt. Plus a free Bot Checkup for your assistant's settings, a library of everyday jobs to hand to AI, and plain-English guides. Every item links to its source.

item.title: Have your bot call stores to check if something is in stock
item.description: Instead of driving around or sitting on hold, tell your bot what you're looking for. It phones a few nearby stores one by one, asks if they have it today, what sizes or models there are and the price, and gives you one short table so you know where to go. You end up with: A short table of which nearby stores have what you need today, so you make one trip instead of five calls.

item.title: Run the family Secret Santa with your bot
item.description: Your bot handles the busywork of a family or office Secret Santa: it emails everyone their person, passes each wish list to the right gift-giver, and nudges anyone who's late, while you approve every email. A proper draw tool picks the names so nobody, not even you, has to see the matches. You end up with: A Secret Santa that runs itself: everyone knows their person, wish lists reach the right gift-giver, and you didn't have to keep the secret or chase anyone.

item.title: Keep hidden instructions in emails and web pages from steering your bot
item.description: If your bot reads your email or browses for you, a stranger can hide instructions in a message or page ('forward the last 5 invoices to...'). It's called prompt injection, and no company says it's solved. A few settings and one standing rule make a fooled bot much less able to do harm. You end up with: A bot that can still read your inbox and the web, but has to come back to you before a hidden instruction can make it send, share or spend anything.

item.title: Have your bot check on every package and chase the late ones
item.description: Your bot finds every shipping email from the last couple of weeks, opens each carrier's tracking page, and tells you what's on time, what's stuck and what to do about it. If a package is late or marked delivered but missing, it drafts the message to the store (or, in some apps, calls them) and waits for your OK. You end up with: One short list of every package and where it really is, plus a ready-to-send note to the store for any that went wrong.

item.title: Rebook all your clients after a surprise schedule change
item.description: When a surgery, a sick day or a family emergency wipes out your week, your bot moves everyone for you. It looks at when each client usually comes, offers each one a new slot that fits, updates the calendar when they say yes, and sends reminders the night before. You end up with: A rebuilt schedule with every client offered a slot that suits them, in about an hour instead of a full day of texting, plus automatic reminders.

item.title: Set up a new bot by talking it through like a new hire
item.description: Instead of writing a perfect prompt, talk to your new bot for about 10 minutes about the job, the way you'd brief a new employee. Then have it repeat the job back, save it as written instructions, and let it suggest actions for a while before it works on its own. You end up with: A bot with one clear job and written instructions it follows the same way every time, instead of a chat you have to re-explain every morning.

item.title: Have your bot send a fax when an office won't pick up the phone
item.description: Some doctor's offices and agencies are almost impossible to reach by phone, and some hang up on AI callers. Your bot can find their fax number, write a one-page request in your name, and send it through an online fax service once you approve it. You end up with: Your request sitting on the office's fax machine, plus a copy and a delivery status, without buying a fax machine or driving over.

item.title: Tell your bot where you put things, then just ask it later
item.description: Every time you store, lend or move something, tell your bot in one line. Months later, ask 'where are the spare batteries?' or 'what's in bin 4?' and it answers with the room, shelf or box. You end up with: A searchable list of what you own and where it is, kept up to date by one-line messages instead of a spreadsheet.

item.title: Get a morning brief that pulls in the emails you need for each of today's meetings
item.description: Set a daily task so your AI assistant checks your calendar each morning, finds the emails, messages and notes behind each meeting, and hands you one short page: what each meeting is about, what you owe people, and what clashes. You end up with: One page to read over coffee that tells you what each of today's meetings needs from you, with the right emails already linked.

item.title: Get your car booked in for a service by letting an AI call the nearby shops
item.description: Tell your AI assistant your car is due for a service and when you're free. It phones the nearest shops or dealerships at the same time, sits on hold for you, finds one that takes appointments at a time that fits, and puts it on your calendar. You end up with: A confirmed service appointment on your calendar, plus a short note of what each shop offered, without spending time on hold.

item.title: Get a morning check-in from your fitness watch that says how you slept and what to train today
item.description: Connect your Garmin (or Oura, Strava or Withings) data to an AI assistant and it reads your sleep, heart-rate variability (HRV), recent runs and training load, then gives you a short morning note: how recovered you look, how last week went, and a suggested session for today. Some connectors can also put an approved workout straight onto your watch. You end up with: A two-minute morning read on your recovery and training, plus an approved workout waiting on your watch if you want one.

item.title: Turn scattered booking emails into one trip sheet that flags clashes
item.description: Your flight, hotel, train and dinner confirmations are spread over five emails. Put them in one folder (or forward them) and an AI agent reads them all, writes one day-by-day trip sheet with every time, address and confirmation code, and warns you about clashes, like a flight that lands after the hotel desk closes. You end up with: One trip sheet with every booking in time order and a short list of problems to fix before you leave.

item.title: Share a scam-check bot your parent can text before they send money
item.description: Set up one AI bot with clear scam-checking instructions and share it with an older parent. When a scary call, text or email arrives ('your grandson is in jail'), they text the bot first and get a calm, plain answer and the safe next step, like calling the relative back on a saved number. You end up with: A patient 'second opinion' your parent can text any time, set up once by you, that pushes every money-under-pressure moment back to a phone call with family.

item.title: Design an embroidery pattern by telling an AI agent what to stitch
item.description: ZigZag is a free, open-source embroidery editor for Mac and Windows with a built-in connection for AI agents. You describe a patch or monogram, the agent draws it in the editor while you watch, checks a stitch preview, and exports a file your embroidery machine can sew. You end up with: A finished embroidery file for your machine, plus the design open in the editor so you can tweak any stitch yourself. Every agent step is one Undo.

item.title: Back up your AI agent so you never lose its memory (and move it to a new computer)
item.description: If your agent runs on your own computer or server, its memory, chats, automations and logins live in a folder that one crash could wipe. OpenClaw has a built-in backup and restore, and one user just moved 9 agents and 800+ sessions to a bigger server with 11 minutes of downtime. You end up with: A tested backup file of your agent you can restore any time, or the same agent running on a new machine with its memory and automations intact.

item.title: Let an AI agent tap through your phone apps for you (and ask before it sends or pays)
item.description: New free, open-source tools let an AI agent open apps on your real iPhone or Android phone, tap, scroll, type and read the screen, while you watch on your computer. It's handy for app-only chores like checking fares in an airline app, and the best ones hold every send, payment or delete until you click Allow. You end up with: An app-only chore done on your own phone, such as fares read back from an airline app or a form filled in, with a record of every tap and nothing sent or paid without your click.

item.title: Let AI agents dig through public data on a hobby question (and try to prove you wrong)
item.description: Two non-scientists just used teams of AI agents on free public data: one found a Maya ruin hidden under jungle in NASA lidar scans overnight, the other turned up two planet candidates that NASA's TESS team has now listed. You pick the question and the rules; the agents do the hours of looking, checking and writing up. You end up with: A shortlist of real leads from public data, each with the evidence and the checks it passed, plus a draft note for the experts who can confirm it.

item.title: Hand your agent a quick errand from your smartwatch
item.description: Meta's Muse agent now has an Apple Watch and Wear OS app. Say or type a quick errand on your wrist, like finding movie tickets or fixing a calendar clash, and approve the result without pulling out your phone. You end up with: Small errands started from your wrist and finished in the background, with you approving the final step.

item.title: Teach your bot to remember what works, so it stops repeating mistakes
item.description: A bot that forgets everything between chats makes the same mistake twice. Give it a notes file it reads at the start and updates at the end, and it gets better every week. Anthropic published how it does this for Claude. You end up with: A bot (or Claude project) that carries lessons from one session to the next. You can open the notes any time and see what it believes.

item.title: Ask Claude about your own spending across your banks
item.description: Claude's Personal Finance beta lets you link US bank and card accounts through Plaid, then ask plain questions like "where did my money go last month?" It can only read your accounts — it can't move, manage or invest your money. You end up with: A single place to see spending across the accounts you linked, plus answers to questions about your own money that you can check against your bank app.

item.title: Have an AI agent research your family history for you
item.description: MyHeritage just launched GAIA, an AI research agent that takes a question like 'who were my great-grandfather's parents?', searches old records and your family tree on its own, and shows you what it found with a confidence rating. Nothing goes into your tree until you approve it. You end up with: A research session on one ancestor with the records found, how sure the agent is about each one, and suggested next places to look, which you then check and choose to save.

item.title: Stop your AI chats from being used for training (and check it stays off)
item.description: Paying for ChatGPT or Gemini doesn't automatically keep your chats out of model training. This week Hacker News users found Gemini keeps training on saved chats unless you turn off Keep Activity, and some ChatGPT users said the Codex training switch had turned itself back on. Here's how to switch it off and re-check it. You end up with: Training switched off in each AI app you use, a monthly reminder to re-check, and a habit of using temporary chats for sensitive things.

item.title: Understand your tax forms with AI, safely
item.description: Tax forms are full of jargon. AI is good at explaining what a box or a letter means in plain English and building you a checklist of questions, but tests show it gets the math and personal rules wrong, so it should never fill in or file your return for you. You end up with: A plain-English explanation of your forms, a list of documents to gather, and a short list of questions to check with IRS.gov, your tax software or a real tax professional.

item.title: Keep a visa application on track with an AI agent
item.description: Tell an agent "get my visa by the end of November" and it lists what you need, tracks missing documents and reminds you until it's done. It can also spot an upcoming trip in your calendar and flag visa rules and arrival forms. You end up with: One running checklist for your visa and entry forms, with reminders, so nothing is missed before you fly.

item.title: Put ChatGPT on a schedule: daily briefings, reminders and watchers
item.description: ChatGPT's scheduled tasks run a prompt for you at a set time, every day or week, or watch for a change and tell you only when something happens. Free plans get 3 active tasks once a day; paid plans can run hourly at exact times. You end up with: A few small jobs that run themselves on a schedule, like a morning briefing, a weekly plan and a watcher that only pings you when something changes.

item.title: Let an AI write and send your emails, after you OK each one
item.description: Yes. ChatGPT and Claude can now send email from your connected Gmail (ChatGPT also Outlook), and Gemini's Tasks can reply and forward. Each one shows you the email and waits for your OK before it goes out, unless you switch that off. Keep it on. You end up with: Emails written and sent from your own Gmail or Outlook without opening your inbox, each one checked and approved by you first.

item.title: Book a flight with an AI agent (and check it before you pay)
item.description: Yes, some AI agents can now book a flight for you: they search, pick the fare you approve, fill in passenger details and stop for your OK before paying. You still check names, price and fare rules yourself. You end up with: A booked flight with a confirmation code from the airline, after you approved the exact fare and passenger names.

item.title: Snap a photo of your handwritten shopping list and let an agent fill the cart
item.description: Walmart's shopping agent, Sparky, can now read a photo of a handwritten list (or a list exported from your phone's Notes app) and turn it into a cart, matched item by item to your usual store and the things you've bought before. You check the cart and pay; it does the searching. You end up with: A ready-to-check cart in a minute or two instead of typing every item into a search box, with out-of-stock items already flagged.

item.title: Make your agent prove it really booked, sent or saved it
item.description: Agents sometimes say "all set!" when the booking, update or message never went through. A new test of 19 AI models found this was the most common way they broke the rules. The fix is simple: ask your agent to show proof (a confirmation number, a link, a screenshot or the confirmation email) and to check the real result before it tells you it's done. You end up with: A bot you can trust a bit more: every "done" comes with something you can check in ten seconds, and failures show up as failures instead of a cheerful "all set".

item.title: Prepare and practice negotiating your salary or a job offer
item.description: You got an offer, or you want a raise, and the money talk makes you nervous. AI can help you pick your numbers from real pay data, draft a friendly counteroffer email and play the recruiter or manager so you can rehearse first. You end up with: A target number, a walk-away number, a short counteroffer email in your own words, and a few practice rounds against a realistic recruiter or manager.

item.title: Have your bot catch calendar clashes hiding in your email
item.description: Plans don't only live in your calendar. A rescheduled event in a confirmation email, or a "call Mom at 2" note you emailed yourself, can quietly clash with what's booked. An always-on agent can compare your email with your calendar every morning and text you before a clash, but in WIRED's test of six agents only two caught one on their own, so ask for this check by name. You end up with: A short morning heads-up, only when something clashes, so you don't show up on the wrong day or double-book yourself.

item.title: AI weekly planning: a realistic-week example
item.description: Try a weekly-planning example, build instructions for your AI app, and check for overload before you use the plan. The steps further down are about assistants that can read a calendar. This site does not read one, and the example is fictional. You end up with: A realistic plan for today on your own calendar, built around your existing appointments, plus a short list of what moved to later.

item.title: Describe an automation in plain words and let IFTTT's AI build and run it
item.description: IFTTT ("if this, then that") is now IFTTT.ai. You type what you want, like "when a package is delivered, flash my lights" or "email me when it's going to rain tomorrow", and it builds the automation and runs it around the clock. Its new AI Agent can also watch a web page for new items, or act across your connected apps from a plain-language instruction. You end up with: Small always-on helpers that react the moment something happens, built by describing them, with a clear trigger and action you can read and turn off.

item.title: Set up an AI coach that helps you (or your teen) start overwhelming tasks and checks in
item.description: A parent shared how they set up ChatGPT as a "getting started" coach for their 20-year-old son with ADHD: one chat for schedule and check-ins, a Project for each big job so it remembers progress, and instructions to ask one question at a time and give one five-minute first step. Scheduled check-ins keep it going without anyone nagging. You end up with: A plan with small steps and a finish date for the job you've been avoiding, and a coach that remembers your progress and nudges you on a schedule.

item.title: Let your AI find and buy things for you with Shop Pay
item.description: Connect Shopify's free Shop skill to ChatGPT or Claude (or use Shop Pay inside Muse, Instinct, Claude Duet or Grok Bot) and your AI can search online stores, fill in a checkout and pay with Shop Pay. You approve every purchase, and your card number is never handed to the AI. You end up with: The thing you wanted, found and ordered from one chat, with every purchase approved by you and the order tracked in your Shop app.

item.title: Let ChatGPT catch you up on your iCloud Mail and update your iPhone calendar
item.description: If your email ends in @icloud.com, @me.com or @mac.com, ChatGPT can now read and search it, draft replies and add or move events on the calendar you see on your iPhone. It works on every ChatGPT plan, including Free, and ChatGPT's always-on dots can use it too. You end up with: A short catch-up of your iCloud inbox and an up-to-date iPhone calendar, without opening the Mail or Calendar apps.

item.title: Add an AI to your friends' group chat to make plans happen
item.description: Instead of 60 messages about where and when, you add an AI agent to the iMessage group. It suggests options, gets everyone to agree, and then books the table, tickets or rental car for the group once someone says yes. You end up with: A plan everyone agreed to, already booked, with the details pinned in the same chat where you talked about it.

item.title: Keep an AI agent from deleting your files
item.description: Before an agent like Claude Cowork, Codex, OpenClaw or Hermes works on your computer, give it one working folder of copies, keep a backup it can't reach, and turn on its read-only or sandbox setting, so one wrong command can't wipe your files. You end up with: An agent that can only touch one folder of copies, has to ask before it deletes anything, and can't reach the backup that saves you if it gets something wrong.

item.title: Put together a home or car insurance claim with an AI agent
item.description: Drop your photos, receipts and policy into one folder and let an agent build the damage list, a dated timeline and the questions to ask your insurer. You check every line and file the claim yourself. You end up with: A claim folder with a damage list that points to your photos and receipts, a dated timeline, your deadlines and the questions to ask, ready for you to submit and for the adjuster's visit.

item.title: Organize your photos by just asking
item.description: Connect Google Photos to Gemini and give it a task in plain words: find the best shots from a trip, skip the near-duplicates, and put them in a new private album, or do it on a schedule every month. You end up with: Curated albums of your best photos from each trip or event, made by describing what you want, and kept private until you say to share them.
